metadata.document: RESTORING TE PĀTAKA O RĀKAIHAUTŪ BANKS PENINSULA

cleaned_body_text: RESTORING TE PĀTAKA O RĀKAIHAUTŪ BANKS PENINSULA Raewyn Peart and Cordelia Woodhouse. First published February 2021. Published by Environmental Defence Society Incorporated. We would like to acknowledge the support of Environment Canterbury in funding this case study. Banks Peninsula, the largest true peninsula in New Zealand, is located on the east coast of the South Island within the Canterbury region. The Peninsula is around 50km long and 30km wide, covering an area of approximately 1,120km2. It is an iconic landscape featuring two ancient volcanic cones and associated lava flows. The Peninsula has a rugged topography with more than 100 short and often very steep catchments. Formerly perhaps up to 3,000m high, the landform now ranges from sea level to around 920m in height. Many of the summits on the Peninsula exceed 500m. Farm restructuring during the 1980s reversed the trend of land clearance and increased stocking. The cost of maintaining new marginal pastures proved uneconomic, land was left to revert to scrub, and stocking rates were reduced. During the 2000s, restoration on Banks Peninsula evolved from individual property efforts into landscape-scale initiatives where mana whenua, landowners, not-for-profit entities and government agencies pooled their efforts. This has enabled results to be scaled up significantly. Farming systems on Banks Peninsula are closely linked to the natural attributes of the land, soil and climate. Tourism has become increasingly important to the economy of Banks Peninsula, particularly in Akaroa and surrounding rural communities. The RMA is currently the primary legislative tool for the management of New Zealand's environment and resources. Banks Peninsula is a unique and iconic landscape, quite different to anywhere else in the country. Its very steep and deeply incised terrain has created a vast array of microclimes which support rare and endemic species. Overall, there is considerable potential on Banks Peninsula to continue to heal the land and create a thriving, biodiverse and sustainable working landscape that supports the community and nature.
